course.description: SAMPLE DATA. A study of fundamental data structures and algorithms, including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, graphs, sorting, searching, and algorithm analysis.

course_outcomes.text: Explain the properties, operations, and trade-offs of fundamental data structures.
Analyze the time and space complexity of algorithms using asymptotic notation.
Implement linear and non-linear data structures in a programming language.
Apply sorting, searching, and graph algorithms to solve computational problems.
Demonstrate disciplined, collaborative, and ethical practices in software development.

weekly_schedule.topic: Course Overview and Algorithm Analysis Basics
weekly_schedule.description: Course orientation, abstract data types, and the idea of measuring algorithm efficiency.

lesson_outcomes.text: Define abstract data type and explain why data structure choice affects efficiency.
Measure the running time of a simple algorithm for increasing input sizes.
Demonstrate commitment to course policies on academic integrity and collaboration.

weekly_schedule.description: Big-O, Omega, and Theta notation; analyzing loops and recursion.

lesson_outcomes.text: Explain Big-O, Omega, and Theta notation.
Determine the time complexity of iterative code fragments.
Justify complexity claims with clear reasoning rather than guesswork.

weekly_schedule.description: Static and dynamic arrays, string operations, and common array algorithms.

lesson_outcomes.text: Describe the memory layout and access cost of arrays.
Implement a dynamic array that resizes automatically.
Practice careful testing of boundary cases such as empty and full arrays.

weekly_schedule.description: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists with insertion and deletion.

lesson_outcomes.text: Compare linked lists with arrays in terms of insertion, deletion, and access cost.
Implement a singly linked list with insert, delete, and search operations.
Demonstrate diligence in debugging pointer and reference errors.

weekly_schedule.description: The stack ADT and its applications such as expression evaluation.

lesson_outcomes.text: Explain the last-in, first-out behavior of the stack ADT.
Apply a stack to evaluate postfix expressions and check balanced parentheses.
Collaborate with a partner during pair-programming exercises.

weekly_schedule.description: Queue, circular queue, deque, and priority queue basics.

lesson_outcomes.text: Differentiate queues, deques, and priority queues by their operations.
Implement a circular queue using an array.
Reflect on design trade-offs when selecting a linear data structure.

weekly_schedule.description: Recursive problem solving, base cases, and call stack behavior.

lesson_outcomes.text: Describe the roles of the base case and recursive case in a recursive function.
Write recursive solutions for factorial, Fibonacci, and binary search.
Show perseverance in tracing recursive calls to locate logic errors.
Explain how bubble, selection, and insertion sort order a list.
Implement insertion sort and count its comparisons on sample inputs.
Practice honest reporting of experimental results, including unfavorable ones.

weekly_schedule.description: Review of Weeks 1 to 8 and midterm assessment.

lesson_outcomes.text: Recall the properties of arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues.
Solve complexity analysis and data structure problems under timed conditions.
Demonstrate academic integrity during the examination.

weekly_schedule.topic: Sorting II: Merge Sort and Quick Sort
weekly_schedule.description: Divide-and-conquer sorting with analysis of best, average, and worst cases.

lesson_outcomes.text: Explain the divide-and-conquer strategy used by merge sort and quick sort.
Implement merge sort and quick sort and compare their running times.
Defend algorithm choices using complexity analysis and measured data.

weekly_schedule.description: Linear and binary search, hash functions, and collision resolution.

lesson_outcomes.text: Describe how hash functions and collision resolution strategies work.
Implement a hash table using separate chaining.
Practice writing readable, documented code for team use.

weekly_schedule.description: Tree terminology, traversals, and binary search tree operations.

lesson_outcomes.text: Define tree terminology and describe inorder, preorder, and postorder traversals.
Implement a binary search tree with insert, search, and traversal operations.
Demonstrate responsibility by testing code before submitting it.

weekly_schedule.description: AVL trees, rotations, and binary heaps.

lesson_outcomes.text: Explain why balancing keeps search tree operations efficient.
Implement a binary min-heap and use it to build a priority queue.
Show initiative in consulting documentation to resolve implementation issues.

weekly_schedule.description: Adjacency lists and matrices, breadth-first and depth-first traversal.

lesson_outcomes.text: Compare adjacency list and adjacency matrix representations of a graph.
Implement breadth-first and depth-first traversal on a graph.
Collaborate effectively to model real-world networks as graphs.

weekly_schedule.description: Dijkstra's algorithm and an introduction to minimum spanning trees.

lesson_outcomes.text: Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in weighted graphs.
Implement Dijkstra's algorithm using a priority queue.
Justify the choice of algorithm for a given network problem.

weekly_schedule.description: Greedy algorithms and an introduction to dynamic programming.

lesson_outcomes.text: Distinguish greedy algorithms from dynamic programming by their problem requirements.
Solve the coin change problem using a dynamic programming approach.
Demonstrate perseverance when decomposing problems into subproblems.

weekly_schedule.topic: Applied Problem Solving and Algorithm Selection
weekly_schedule.description: Selecting suitable data structures and algorithms for practical scenarios.

lesson_outcomes.text: Identify the data structure and algorithm best suited to a described scenario.
Develop a program that combines at least two data structures to solve a practical problem.
Practice ethical use of references and open-source code, with proper credit.
Summarize the data structures and algorithms used in the final project.
Demonstrate a working program and explain its time and space complexity.
Accept feedback professionally and reflect on areas for improvement.
